body:
This is expected. The fallback to OpenGL is more like a last resort rather than something that is expected to seamlessly handle any device. The reason is that it is very naively implemented and designed around desktop devices which fail more gracefully. 

The problem on mobile is that, for many devices, when you try to enable Vulkan, they will begin to run and then crash immediately. If the engine crashes, we can't gracefully fall back to OpenGL. On Desktop, devices that don't support Vulkan (or don't support the version of Vulkan that we need) will instead throw an error. We can detect those errors and then fallback to OpenGL as a last resort. 

However, in general, falling back to OpenGL is quite bad since we don't have feature parity between the Mobile renderer and the Compatibility renderer and the two renderers can look quite different in certain situations. Accordingly, even if we fall back, it might totally break your game anyway. So the fallback mechanism shouldn't be relied upon by most games. 

Therefore, I think we should do the folllowing:
1. Update the documentation to be more clear about the limitations of the fallback mechanism
2. Add a ".mobile" override for the "fallback to opengl" setting and default it to "false" so Mobile doesn't attempt to fall back. 

Ultimately, the manifest is there to protect you. If you try to run your game with the Mobile renderer (even with the fallback enabled), you will get a lot of crashes and ANR errors that will result in your game being penalized by Google Play. In order to ensure the best experience for your players, you need to make use of the manifest file to exclude devices that don't support the minimum features required, or design your game for the Compatibility renderer from the beginning

Updating the documentation makes sense to me. I'm not 100% certain I understand what benefits disabling fallback on mobile would have - but at least if it's a setting we can just adjust it for the best results we can achieve.

As a slight aside:

> Ultimately, the manifest is there to protect you. If you try to run your game with the Mobile renderer (even with the fallback enabled), you will get a lot of crashes and ANR errors that will result in your game being penalized by Google Play. In order to ensure the best experience for your players, you need to make use of the manifest file to exclude devices that don't support the minimum features required, or design your game for the Compatibility renderer from the beginning

Frustratingly enough, we have been getting crash reports on Android when using `gl_compatibility` on some new flagship models (e.g. Google Pixel 10 Pro XL), so we are currently using `mobile` on Android. (No bug report created for this yet since we don't have this device available to test & corroborate with.)
And on iOS we are forced to using `gl_compatibility` since `mobile` crashes on older devices due to the fallback detection not working on older devices (and the project launched without having set some requirements we can't change post-launch).

Are you using particle shaders? This may be what https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111329 aims to work around for PowerVR GPUs (like the Pixel 10 Pro's).

> The problem on mobile is that, for many devices, when you try to enable Vulkan, they will begin to run and then crash immediately

As I mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/discussions/12166#discussioncomment-15222481, raising the Vulkan version requirement to 1.1 on mobile platforms could help reduce the number of cases where GPUs try to initialize Vulkan then crash immediately after. As far as I know, all Android devices with acceptable Vulkan support feature 1.1 at least (probably 1.2 nowadays, in fact).

If the GPU only supports Vulkan 1.0, falling back to OpenGL immediately without trying to fully initialize Vulkan could avoid a crash.
Together with issue https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/109550 it prevents to have broad supported devices and screenshots from emulation both.
